props.title: Sylvia Scarlett
props.initialSlug: Cross-dressing heiress finds love in wild con game

sections.content: Sylvia Scarlett (1935) stands as one of classic Hollywood's boldest experiments in gender performance, featuring Katharine Hepburn disguising herself as a boy to help her father escape trouble. Director George Cukor, who would later helm The Philadelphia Story (1940) and Adam's Rib (1949), brings a sophisticated touch to this ahead-of-its-time exploration of gender fluidity. The film's commercial failure actually freed Hepburn and Cukor to take more risks, leading to their legendary collaboration spanning decades. Cary Grant delivers one of his earliest scene-stealing performances here, showing glimpses of the charming rogue persona he'd perfect in films like Bringing Up Baby (1938).

sections.content: The theme of cross-dressing and gender performance runs through cinema history, from Some Like It Hot (1959) to Tootsie (1982). But while many of these later films played gender switching primarily for laughs, Sylvia Scarlett dared to explore the genuine emotional and social implications of its protagonist's transformation. The film's exploration of attraction and identity was remarkably progressive for its era, particularly in scenes where characters find themselves drawn to Sylvia both as male and female personas.

Cukor's direction shows remarkable sensitivity in handling the material, drawing on techniques he'd later perfect in films like A Star Is Born (1954). The camera work subtly shifts between treating Sylvia as masculine or feminine depending on the scene's requirements, while Hepburn's performance captures both the freedom and constraint of gender performance. This sophisticated approach influenced later works like Boys Don't Cry (1999) and Albert Nobbs (2011). SUBHEAD: Gender Performance in Classic Hollywood

sections.content: While Sylvia Scarlett struggled at the box office, it established important precedents for how Hollywood could handle complex gender themes. The film's influence can be traced through works like I Was a Male War Bride (1949) and Glen or Glenda (1953), leading eventually to more nuanced modern explorations like The Danish Girl (2015). Hepburn's commanding performance helped establish her signature strength and independence, traits that would define her later roles in films like Woman of the Year (1942).
